visual_prompts.vision:
You are shown a single image containing still frames sampled at even intervals
across one learner's recorded presentation, in order from the start of the talk
to the end. There are six of them and they are six separate moments, not
continuous video.

Report ONLY what is visible. Do not score, rate or evaluate anything. Do not
guess at what is not visible. Reporting that you cannot tell is more useful than
a confident guess.

In "note", write four to six sentences of plain prose covering:
- what the hands and arms are doing, and whether that changes across the frames;
- posture and stance, and any repeated movement such as rocking, pacing or
  fidgeting;
- where the eyes appear to be directed, for example toward the camera, downward
  at notes, or off to one side;
- how the speaker is framed: how much of them is in shot, whether the hands are
  in view, and whether the face is lit well enough to read.

Say how many of the six frames each observation is based on. Do not write
"throughout", "for most of the talk" or "consistently": you have six moments and
you cannot see what happened between them.

Never write about the speaker's appearance, face or body except as it bears on
the four points above. Never write about ethnicity, race, age, gender, build,
health, disability, hair, clothing, jewellery or religious dress. Never write
about the room, the background, or anything in it. Never read or transcribe text
in the image. If another person is visible, ignore them completely and report
only on the speaker.

In "unusable_frames", give how many of the frames are too dark, too blurred, too
distant, or cropped so that the hands or the face cannot be seen.

In "confidence", answer "high" when at least four frames are readable and the
hands and face are in shot, "medium" when the frames are readable but part of
the speaker is out of shot, and "low" when three or more frames are unusable.
visual_prompts.vision_user: Report what is visible in these frames now.
visual_prompts.summary_english:
VISUAL SUMMARY. Also produce "visual_summary": two or three sentences, at most
60 words, written to the learner in the second person, saying what the visual
evidence above shows about their presentation. This is the only part of the
visual evidence the learner will ever read, so write it as the plain-language
version of that evidence, not as a repeat of your criterion comments.

Write only about things the learner can do differently in their next recording:
what their hands and arms did, their posture and stance, any repeated movement,
where they were looking, how much of them was in shot, and whether the light let
their face be read. Tie each observation to its effect on the presentation. For
example: "your hands stayed below the desk in every frame, so your gestures were
hard to see".

The evidence comes from six still frames, not from continuous video, so do not
write "throughout", "for most of the talk" or "consistently".

Never write about the learner's appearance, face, body, build, hair, clothing,
jewellery, religious dress, age, gender, ethnicity, race, accent, health or
disability. Never write about the room, the background, or anything in it. Never
describe anyone else who is visible. Never state or guess how the learner was
feeling, or what kind of person they are. Never quote the visual evidence text
directly. Never give a number or a score.

Write it in English.

If the visual evidence does not support two sentences of this kind, write one
and stop. If it supports none, return an empty string.

slide_vision_prompt.informative: You are a supportive presentation-design coach. You are shown the slide images from a learner's informative presentation (a bounded sample if the deck is long). Comment ONLY on the visual design of the slides: layout, visual hierarchy, text density, readability, consistency, and use of visuals. Do not judge the spoken delivery or transcribe the text. Give two or three sentences of encouraging, concrete feedback naming one clear strength and the single highest-leverage visual improvement. Plain prose, no headings, no lists.

ptype_hint.persuasive: This is a PERSUASIVE presentation: the learner is trying to convince the audience. Weight your feedback toward a clear position or claim, the strength of evidence and reasoning, use of rhetorical appeals (credibility, logic, and emotion), acknowledging counter-arguments, and a clear call to action. Reward a well-supported argument over neutral description.
ptype_hint.informative: This is an INFORMATIVE presentation: the learner is explaining or teaching. Weight your feedback toward clarity of explanation, accuracy, logical organization, coverage of the topic, and helping the audience understand. Do not expect a persuasive thesis or a call to action.
ptype_hint.Informative: This is an INFORMATIVE presentation: the learner is explaining or teaching. Weight your feedback toward clarity of explanation, accuracy, logical organization, coverage of the topic, and helping the audience understand. Do not expect a persuasive thesis or a call to action.
ptype_hint.practice: This is a PRACTICE presentation: a short, low-stakes talk, often the learner introducing themselves. Keep the feedback warm and encouraging, praise what worked first, and give one small, concrete next step per criterion. Do not expect sources, a thesis or a call to action.
ptype_hint.entertain: This is a SPEECH TO ENTERTAIN: the learner is trying to engage and delight the audience while still making a point. Weight your feedback toward storytelling, vivid language, well-timed humor suited to the audience, a clear central idea, and an organized arc from opening to close. Do not expect formal sources or a call to action.

default_criteria.name: Structure & Organization
default_criteria.description: Clear opening, logical flow of ideas, and a strong close.

default_criteria.name: Content & Relevance

default_criteria.name: Language & Vocabulary

default_criteria.name: Time Management

visual_criteria.name: Body Language & Gestures
visual_criteria.description: Gestures, posture and movement that SUPPORT what you are saying: open hands that mark structure or add emphasis, a steady stance, and weight that stays settled. No repeated habits that DISTRACT from the presentation (fidgeting, rocking or pacing, hands in pockets or folded, or playing with an object).

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Gestures, posture and movement consistently support the message: open, purposeful gestures mark structure or emphasis, the stance is steady, and no habit distracts.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Gestures and posture mostly support the message, with a minor distracting habit at times.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some purposeful gestures, but a repeated habit (fidgeting, rocking or pacing) sometimes distracts.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Few purposeful gestures, and distracting habits are frequent.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Body language works against the message in most of the frames.

visual_criteria.name: Eye Contact & Camera Presence
visual_criteria.description: Looking at the camera lens as if it were your audience, rather than reading from notes or watching a second screen. Steady head-and-shoulders framing that keeps your hands in view, a face lit well enough to read, and facial expression that matches what you are saying.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Looks at the camera lens as if it were the audience nearly all the time, with framing, lighting and facial expression that support the message.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Mostly looks at the lens, with some glances at notes, and good framing and lighting.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Looks at the lens about half the time, or the framing or lighting makes the face hard to read in places.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Mostly looks away from the lens (at notes or another screen), or the face is often hard to see.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Rarely looks at the lens, or can't be seen clearly.

criteria.name: Language & Vocabulary

esl_beginner.hint: The learner is a beginner-level English-as-a-second-language student. Prioritise intelligibility and communication over native-like accuracy. Use simple, clear language in your feedback, warmly praise successful communication, and give one small, concrete improvement per criterion. Do not penalise a noticeable accent.

criteria.name: Pronunciation & Intelligibility
criteria.description: Sounds, word stress, and being understood by a patient listener.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Easy to understand throughout. Sounds and word stress are clear enough that a listener rarely has to guess, and an accent is fine.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Understood almost all the time. A few words are unclear, but the meaning comes through.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Understood with some effort. Several words are mispronounced in ways that slow the listener down.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Often hard to understand. Many words have to be guessed from context.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Mostly not understandable, even to a patient listener.

criteria.name: Fluency & Pace
criteria.description: Speaking in connected phrases without long pauses or heavy hesitation.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Speaks in connected phrases and short sentences with natural pauses, and keeps going.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Mostly connected phrases. Some hesitation, but the talk keeps moving.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Frequent pauses and restarts, but most ideas are finished.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Mostly single words or short fragments with long pauses.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Too few words or too many long silences to follow.

criteria.name: Basic Grammar
criteria.description: Simple tenses, subject-verb agreement, and word order.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Simple present and past tenses, subject-verb agreement and basic word order are mostly correct, and errors don't block the meaning.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Basic structures are usually right, with some errors in tense or agreement.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Errors in basic tenses, agreement or word order are frequent, but the meaning is mostly clear.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Errors in basic structures often make the meaning unclear.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Little control of basic sentence structure yet.

criteria.name: Core Vocabulary
criteria.description: Using common, topic-relevant words and getting meaning across despite gaps.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Uses common, topic-relevant words well and finds a way around gaps, for example by describing a word.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Enough everyday words for the topic, with an occasional wrong word or repetition.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: A limited set of words, often repeated or sometimes wrong, but the main meaning comes through.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Vocabulary is so limited that the meaning is often lost.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Too few words yet to talk about the topic.

criteria.name: Task Completion
criteria.description: Staying on topic and saying enough on the prompt to be understood.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Stays on topic and says enough to answer the prompt fully, with a simple example or detail.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Stays on topic and answers the prompt, with little detail.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Partly answers the prompt or drifts off topic at times.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Says very little about the prompt.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Doesn't address the prompt yet.

esl_intermediate.hint: The learner is an intermediate-level English-as-a-second-language student. Balance encouragement with targeted correction: acknowledge what works, then name a couple of concrete, level-appropriate improvements (a grammar pattern, a clearer transition, a more precise word). Stretch them slightly beyond their comfort without overwhelming them.

criteria.name: Pronunciation & Clarity
criteria.description: Mostly clear sounds and stress; occasional slips that rarely block understanding.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Clear sounds, word stress and sentence stress. Slips are rare and never block understanding.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Mostly clear, with occasional slips in sounds or stress that rarely affect the meaning.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Generally clear, but repeated errors in some sounds or in stress make the listener work at times.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Frequent errors in sounds or stress often make words hard to catch.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Pronunciation regularly prevents understanding.

criteria.name: Fluency & Pace
criteria.description: Reasonably smooth with some hesitation; keeps going through most ideas.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Speaks smoothly at a steady pace, with little hesitation and quick recovery from mistakes.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Reasonably smooth. Some hesitation when reaching for words, but keeps going.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Noticeable pauses and restarts interrupt the flow in several places.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Frequent long pauses, and ideas are often left unfinished.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: So halting that it's hard to follow.

criteria.name: Grammar
criteria.description: Common tenses and structures handled with some errors in more complex forms.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Common tenses and structures are accurate, with some successful complex sentences. Errors are few and minor.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Common structures are mostly accurate, with errors in more complex forms.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Errors in common tenses or structures are noticeable, but the meaning is clear.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Frequent errors in common structures sometimes hide the meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Grammar errors make much of the speech unclear.

criteria.name: Vocabulary
criteria.description: Adequate range for the topic, with some reach for less common or precise words.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A good range for the topic, with some precise or less common words used correctly.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: An adequate range for the topic, with occasionally imprecise word choice.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Gets the meaning across, but relies on general, repeated words.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: A limited range, and wrong word choices sometimes confuse the meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Vocabulary is too limited to develop the topic.

criteria.name: Organization & Coherence
criteria.description: Clear main idea, mostly logical ordering, and basic connectors.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A clear main idea, a logical order and a range of connectors (first, however, as a result) that make the talk easy to follow.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: A clear main idea and a mostly logical order, with basic connectors.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: A main idea is there, but the order jumps around or the connectors are repetitive (and, and then).

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: The main idea is hard to identify, with few connectors.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No clear main idea or order.

esl_advanced.hint: The learner is an advanced English-as-a-second-language student. Hold them to a high standard of fluency, range, and accuracy while staying encouraging. Note subtle errors in idiom, register, and complex grammar, and push for more natural, native-like phrasing.

criteria.name: Fluency & Naturalness
criteria.description: Smooth pace, natural rhythm, and self-correction that does not disrupt flow.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Speaks naturally and effortlessly at length, with rhythm and pausing that sound native-like, and seamless self-correction.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Fluent and natural, with occasional hesitation when expressing complex ideas.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Generally fluent, but searching for words or rephrasing interrupts the flow on complex points.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Hesitation is frequent for this level, and the flow is often interrupted.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Fluency is well below an advanced level.

criteria.name: Pronunciation & Stress
criteria.description: Clear sounds plus sentence stress and intonation that carry meaning.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Sentence stress, rhythm and intonation carry meaning and nuance (emphasis, contrast, attitude), and an accent never affects understanding.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Clear, with intonation and stress that mostly support the meaning and only minor lapses.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Clear sounds, but flat or misplaced stress and intonation sometimes blur emphasis or nuance.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Errors in stress and intonation often blur the meaning or the speaker's attitude.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Pronunciation regularly gets in the way of the meaning.

criteria.name: Grammatical Range & Accuracy
criteria.description: Varied, complex structures used accurately.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A wide range of complex structures (conditionals, the passive, relative clauses) used accurately and flexibly, with only rare slips.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Varied complex structures, mostly accurate, with occasional errors that don't affect the meaning.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some complex structures attempted, with noticeable errors or a fallback to simpler forms.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Mostly simple structures, with frequent errors in complex forms.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Grammatical control is well below an advanced level.

criteria.name: Vocabulary & Idiom
criteria.description: Precise, varied, idiomatic word choice and appropriate register.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Precise, varied and idiomatic language in a register that fits the audience and purpose (formal, academic or conversational) and shifts deliberately.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: A wide, mostly precise vocabulary with some idiomatic use, and an appropriate register with minor lapses.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: An adequate range, but word choice is sometimes imprecise or unidiomatic, or the register slips (too casual or too stiff).

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Limited precision and frequent mismatches of register.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Vocabulary and register are well below an advanced level.

criteria.name: Coherence & Development
criteria.description: Well-organized ideas with connectors and full development.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Ideas are fully developed and tightly connected, with cohesive devices (reference, substitution, discourse markers) that guide the listener through complex reasoning.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Well organized and developed, with mostly effective cohesive devices.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Organized, but the development is uneven or the connectors are mechanical or overused.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Ideas are loosely connected or underdeveloped.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Little coherence: ideas don't build on one another.

criteria.description: Says who you are and shares a few details (where you're from, what you do or study, an interest) in a way that's easy to follow.

levels.description: A friendly, clear introduction with your name, several specific details and a personal touch that makes you memorable.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: A clear introduction with your name and a few details about you.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Your name and a detail or two, but the introduction is brief or a little hard to follow.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Only your name or a single detail, so listeners don't get to know you yet.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Not an introduction of yourself yet. Try saying your name and two things about you.

criteria.name: Organization
criteria.description: A simple beginning, middle and end, so listeners can follow along.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A clear beginning, middle and end, with ideas in a sensible order and a friendly close.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: The beginning, middle and end are easy to spot, though one part could be smoother.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Ideas are mostly in order, but the start or the end is missing or abrupt.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Ideas jump around, so the talk is hard to follow.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Not organized yet. Try planning one opening line, two or three points and one closing line.

criteria.name: Delivery
criteria.description: Speaking clearly at a comfortable pace, with energy and few fillers.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Clear, confident and at a comfortable pace, with natural energy and almost no fillers.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Clear and easy to follow, with a few fillers or rushed moments.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Mostly understandable, but the pace, long pauses or fillers sometimes get in the way.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Often hard to follow because of the pace, long pauses or many fillers.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Not clear enough to follow yet. Try saying it out loud once before you record.

informative.hint: The learner is practising a general spoken presentation; focus your feedback on presentation and public-speaking skills.

criteria.name: Introduction
criteria.description: An attention-getter clearly linked to the topic, a reason for the audience to listen, the speaker's credibility on the topic, the purpose or thesis, and a preview of the main points.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A vivid attention-getter clearly tied to the topic, a strong reason to listen, credibility made explicit, a clear thesis, and a preview that names every main point.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: An effective attention-getter linked to the topic, a clear thesis and a preview, with the reason to listen or the credibility brief or only implied.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: An opening and a topic are there, but the link to the topic, the reason to listen or the credibility is weak, and the thesis or preview is vague.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Little attempt to gain attention. The topic is named, but there's no clear thesis or preview.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No recognizable introduction: the speech starts straight into content, or its purpose can't be identified.

criteria.name: Organization and transitions
criteria.description: A clear transition into the body, main points that are clear and match the preview, a recognizable pattern, and signposts, internal previews and reviews that keep the audience oriented.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Main points match the preview and follow a recognizable pattern. A smooth transition into the body and consistent signposts, internal previews and reviews make the structure easy to follow.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Main points are clear and mostly match the preview. Transitions and signposts are there, with an occasional abrupt shift.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Main points can be picked out, but the pattern is loose or strays from the preview, and transitions are few or repetitive.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Points are hard to tell apart, with few transitions or signposts, so the audience has to work out the structure.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No clear organization: ideas run together with no transitions.

criteria.name: Support and sources
criteria.description: Credible sources cited orally with enough context to judge them, summary, paraphrase and quotation used accurately and ethically, and evidence in varied forms such as examples, statistics and testimony.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Several credible sources, each cited orally with who they are and why they're credible. Quotation, paraphrase and summary are used accurately and ethically, and varied evidence supports every main point.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Credible sources are cited orally for most points, with some context. Evidence is mostly varied and used ethically.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some support, but sources are cited without context, or the evidence is all of one kind or thin for some points.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Little evidence. Sources aren't named or are unclear, or quoted material isn't clearly attributed.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No supporting evidence or sources: claims rest on opinion alone.

criteria.name: Language
criteria.description: Language that is economical, precise and vivid, and adapted to the audience and the occasion.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Precise, concise and vivid wording, well adapted to the audience and the occasion, with any technical terms explained.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Clear, appropriate language with some vivid moments, and only minor wordiness or imprecision.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Generally understandable, but wordy, vague or repetitive in places, or not always suited to the audience.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Often vague or repetitive, or too casual or too technical for the audience, which gets in the way of the meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The language often hides the message or doesn't suit the occasion.

criteria.name: Delivery
criteria.description: Vocal variety in pace and emphasis, few fillers (um, uh, like), and notes used as reminders rather than read word for word, so the speech sounds spoken to the audience. Gestures and eye contact are judged separately, as body language feedback.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Fluent and conversational, with varied pace and emphasis that bring out the key ideas and almost no fillers. It sounds spoken to the audience, not read.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Mostly fluent and natural, with some variety, and a few fillers or brief stumbles that don't distract.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Understandable, but the pace or emphasis is flat in places, fillers are noticeable, or parts sound read.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Frequent fillers, long pauses or a flat pace, or most of the speech sounds read, which makes it hard to follow.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The delivery gets in the way of the message: very halting, read throughout, or hard to understand.

criteria.name: Conclusion
criteria.description: A clear signal that the speech is ending, the thesis restated and the main points reviewed in fresh language, the importance of the topic re-established, and an effective closing device.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A clear signal of the ending, the thesis restated and every main point reviewed in fresh words, a reminder of why the topic matters, and a memorable closing line.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: A signal of the ending and a summary of the main points, with a less developed closing line or reminder of why the topic matters.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: A conclusion is there, but it's abrupt, repeats the introduction word for word, or reviews only some of the points.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: The speech trails off with a brief "that's it" or a single closing sentence.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No conclusion: the speech simply stops.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: An opening and a topic, but the credibility, why it matters to the audience, the thesis or the preview is vague or missing.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Little attempt to gain attention or connect with the audience, and the position isn't clear.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No recognizable introduction or position.

criteria.name: Organization and transitions

levels.label: Excellent

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: A recognizable pattern and clear transitions, with an occasional abrupt shift.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: The arguments can be picked out, but the pattern is loose and transitions are few.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: The arguments run together, so the audience has to work out the structure.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No clear organization.

criteria.name: Support and sources

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Every main point is clearly stated and backed by enough varied evidence. Sources are introduced efficiently with their credibility, and quotation, summary and paraphrase are handled ethically.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Main points are supported with credible, mostly varied evidence and clear oral citations.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some points lack enough evidence, the evidence is all of one kind, or sources are named without their credibility.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Little evidence, and sources are unclear or not attributed.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Claims rest on opinion alone, with no evidence or sources.

criteria.name: Language
criteria.description: Language adapted to the occasion and the audience, with vivid, dramatic wording that appeals to the senses or feelings.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Vivid, dramatic language that appeals to the senses and feelings, precisely adapted to the audience and the occasion.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Clear, appropriate language with some vivid, persuasive wording.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Clear but plain language, or not always suited to the audience or the occasion.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Vague or repetitive language, or wording that doesn't suit the audience.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The language undermines the argument or doesn't suit the occasion.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Understandable, but the pace or emphasis is flat in places, fillers are noticeable, or parts sound read.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Frequent fillers, long pauses or a flat pace, or most of the speech sounds read, which makes it hard to follow.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The delivery gets in the way of the message: very halting, read throughout, or hard to understand.

criteria.name: Conclusion
criteria.description: A review of the main points and the thesis restated, the audience reconnected to why the topic matters, and a memorable closing statement with a course of action or a call to respond.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A review of the arguments and the thesis restated, a reminder of why it matters to this audience, and a memorable call to action.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: A clear ending that reviews the arguments and asks the audience to act, though the closing line could be stronger.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: A conclusion with a partial review, or a call to action that's vague.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: An abrupt ending with no clear call to action.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No conclusion: the speech simply stops.

criteria.name: Persuasive appeals
criteria.description: A variety of appeals (logical, ethical and emotional), reasoning that avoids fallacies, and points and evidence tailored to the audience.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A skillful mix of logical, ethical and emotional appeals tailored to this audience, with sound reasoning and no fallacies.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: At least two kinds of appeal used well and mostly tailored to the audience, with sound reasoning.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Relies mostly on one kind of appeal, or is only loosely tailored to the audience, or the reasoning has a weak link.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Thin or generic appeals, or an argument that rests on a fallacy such as a sweeping generalization.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No real attempt to persuade, or reasoning that is mostly fallacious.

criteria_visual_general.description: Pace, clarity, confidence, and smoothness of speaking.

criteria_visual_general.description: Clear opening, logical flow of ideas, and a strong close.

criteria_visual_general.name: Time Management
criteria_visual_general.description: Fits the target length without rushing or running long.

criteria_visual_general.name: Body Language & Gestures
criteria_visual_general.description: Gestures, posture and movement that SUPPORT what you are saying: open hands that mark structure or add emphasis, a steady stance, and weight that stays settled. No repeated habits that DISTRACT from the presentation (fidgeting, rocking or pacing, hands in pockets or folded, or playing with an object).

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Gestures, posture and movement consistently support the message: open, purposeful gestures mark structure or emphasis, the stance is steady, and no habit distracts.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Gestures and posture mostly support the message, with a minor distracting habit at times.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some purposeful gestures, but a repeated habit (fidgeting, rocking or pacing) sometimes distracts.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Few purposeful gestures, and distracting habits are frequent.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Body language works against the message in most of the frames.

criteria_visual_general.name: Eye Contact & Camera Presence
criteria_visual_general.description: Looking at the camera lens as if it were your audience, rather than reading from notes or watching a second screen. Steady head-and-shoulders framing that keeps your hands in view, a face lit well enough to read, and facial expression that matches what you are saying.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Looks at the camera lens as if it were the audience nearly all the time, with framing, lighting and facial expression that support the message.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Mostly looks at the lens, with some glances at notes, and good framing and lighting.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Looks at the lens about half the time, or the framing or lighting makes the face hard to read in places.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Mostly looks away from the lens (at notes or another screen), or the face is often hard to see.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Rarely looks at the lens, or can't be seen clearly.

rubric.hint_esl_beginner: The learner is a beginner-level English-as-a-second-language student. Prioritise intelligibility and communication over native-like accuracy. Use simple, clear language in your feedback, warmly praise successful communication, and give one small, concrete improvement per criterion. Do not penalise a noticeable accent.

criteria_esl_beginner.name: Pronunciation & Intelligibility
criteria_esl_beginner.description: Sounds, word stress, and being understood by a patient listener.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Easy to understand throughout. Sounds and word stress are clear enough that a listener rarely has to guess, and an accent is fine.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Understood almost all the time. A few words are unclear, but the meaning comes through.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Understood with some effort. Several words are mispronounced in ways that slow the listener down.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Often hard to understand. Many words have to be guessed from context.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Mostly not understandable, even to a patient listener.

criteria_esl_beginner.name: Fluency & Pace
criteria_esl_beginner.description: Speaking in connected phrases without long pauses or heavy hesitation.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Speaks in connected phrases and short sentences with natural pauses, and keeps going.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Mostly connected phrases. Some hesitation, but the talk keeps moving.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Frequent pauses and restarts, but most ideas are finished.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Mostly single words or short fragments with long pauses.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Too few words or too many long silences to follow.

criteria_esl_beginner.name: Basic Grammar
criteria_esl_beginner.description: Simple tenses, subject-verb agreement, and word order.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Simple present and past tenses, subject-verb agreement and basic word order are mostly correct, and errors don't block the meaning.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Basic structures are usually right, with some errors in tense or agreement.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Errors in basic tenses, agreement or word order are frequent, but the meaning is mostly clear.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Errors in basic structures often make the meaning unclear.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Little control of basic sentence structure yet.

criteria_esl_beginner.name: Core Vocabulary
criteria_esl_beginner.description: Using common, topic-relevant words and getting meaning across despite gaps.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Uses common, topic-relevant words well and finds a way around gaps, for example by describing a word.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Enough everyday words for the topic, with an occasional wrong word or repetition.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: A limited set of words, often repeated or sometimes wrong, but the main meaning comes through.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Vocabulary is so limited that the meaning is often lost.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Too few words yet to talk about the topic.

criteria_esl_beginner.name: Task Completion
criteria_esl_beginner.description: Staying on topic and saying enough on the prompt to be understood.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Stays on topic and answers the prompt, with little detail.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Partly answers the prompt or drifts off topic at times.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Says very little about the prompt.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Doesn't address the prompt yet.

criteria_informative.name: Introduction
criteria_informative.description: An attention-getter clearly linked to the topic, a reason for the audience to listen, the speaker's credibility on the topic, the purpose or thesis, and a preview of the main points.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: A vivid attention-getter clearly tied to the topic, a strong reason to listen, credibility made explicit, a clear thesis, and a preview that names every main point.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: An effective attention-getter linked to the topic, a clear thesis and a preview, with the reason to listen or the credibility brief or only implied.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: An opening and a topic are there, but the link to the topic, the reason to listen or the credibility is weak, and the thesis or preview is vague.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Little attempt to gain attention. The topic is named, but there's no clear thesis or preview.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No recognizable introduction: the speech starts straight into content, or its purpose can't be identified.

criteria_informative.name: Organization and transitions
criteria_informative.description: A clear transition into the body, main points that are clear and match the preview, a recognizable pattern, and signposts, internal previews and reviews that keep the audience oriented.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Main points match the preview and follow a recognizable pattern. A smooth transition into the body and consistent signposts, internal previews and reviews make the structure easy to follow.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Main points are clear and mostly match the preview. Transitions and signposts are there, with an occasional abrupt shift.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Main points can be picked out, but the pattern is loose or strays from the preview, and transitions are few or repetitive.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Points are hard to tell apart, with few transitions or signposts, so the audience has to work out the structure.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No clear organization: ideas run together with no transitions.

criteria_informative.name: Support and sources
criteria_informative.description: Credible sources cited orally with enough context to judge them, summary, paraphrase and quotation used accurately and ethically, and evidence in varied forms such as examples, statistics and testimony.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Several credible sources, each cited orally with who they are and why they're credible. Quotation, paraphrase and summary are used accurately and ethically, and varied evidence supports every main point.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Credible sources are cited orally for most points, with some context. Evidence is mostly varied and used ethically.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some support, but sources are cited without context, or the evidence is all of one kind or thin for some points.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Little evidence. Sources aren't named or are unclear, or quoted material isn't clearly attributed.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No supporting evidence or sources: claims rest on opinion alone.

criteria_informative.name: Language
criteria_informative.description: Language that is economical, precise and vivid, and adapted to the audience and the occasion.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Precise, concise and vivid wording, well adapted to the audience and the occasion, with any technical terms explained.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Clear, appropriate language with some vivid moments, and only minor wordiness or imprecision.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Generally understandable, but wordy, vague or repetitive in places, or not always suited to the audience.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: Often vague or repetitive, or too casual or too technical for the audience, which gets in the way of the meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The language often hides the message or doesn't suit the occasion.

criteria_informative.name: Delivery

levels.label: Proficient

levels.label: Developing

levels.label: Beginning

levels.label: Not yet

levels.label: Proficient

levels.label: Developing

levels.label: Beginning

levels.label: Not yet

levels.label: Proficient

levels.label: Developing
